A few days ago, a new follower told me: “Boss Qi, I want to trade contracts. I want to flip my life around with one trade—take me down.”

I froze when I heard that. The words were way too familiar—so familiar it was like hearing my past self: $EVAA .

Back then I was brand new to the coin world. I was also hyped up by a line that said, “Contracts are the fastest way to turn things around.” In the end, in less than three days, I didn’t manage to flip—my principal disappeared instead.

What really snapped me out of it was the cold wind after a liquidation.

I sat in front of my computer, staring at that string of zeros, silent like someone nursing a breakup.

Only then did I understand: contracts aren’t “fast money”—they’re just “faster losses.”

Later, I turned it over in my mind: what exactly was it that blew me up?

Was it the market? Luck? Skills? None of them.

It was because I didn’t even understand what risk meant back then.

Until later, when I followed an old veteran in the space—his first sentence woke me up and he scolded me: “If you can’t even set a stop-loss, what are you talking about making money?”

After that day, I officially started learning what it means to survive. You have to understand these three things:

First, leverage is a knife. If you hold it wrong, it’ll turn around and cut you.

I was afraid of losing slowly even with 10x leverage back then. Looking back now, it was basically courting death.

Newbies should stick to low leverage honestly, feel what volatility is like. If you’re not afraid of the market, the market will end up being the one afraid of you.

Second, stop-loss isn’t for other people—it’s for people like you, who are soft-hearted.

I used to love holding positions and “carrying through.” But carrying like that eventually carried me right into a shadow.

Even now, when I’m doing trades with my followers, I force every single one of them to set a stop-loss. Otherwise, I’d rather not trade with them.

Third, the most ruthless thing isn’t the market—it’s the impulse to chase pumps and kill trades.

Every liquidation I’ve had was for the same reason: chasing until I got carried away, selling with a bleeding heart, and then the market kicked me out with one move.

Now when I watch others do this, I can see the liquidation scene ahead of time.

Let me be honest: contracts aren’t something you can’t touch—but you have to know they’re fire.

Someone who knows how to cook can use it to make meals. Someone who doesn’t will just burn down the kitchen.

The people who survive—sooner or later, the market will give them a chance.

The ones who die—won’t even be able to see what a chance looks like.

If you’re getting ready to trade contracts right now, or if the market has already slapped you twice, you really should come talk to me.

Don’t think it’s embarrassing. Every seasoned trader climbs out of the graveyard of beginners. It’s just that some people refuse to admit their mistakes when they die, and some people live and understand.

If you’re willing to start from surviving, I’ll teach you the rest.

subTitle:
Most crypto narratives come and go fast.
One month everyone talks about memecoins. Then #AI . Then #RWA . Then L2s. Then something completely new.
But while the market keeps rotating from one story to another, some protocols continue doing the same thing every day: moving real liquidity, serving real users, and proving that DeFi still has a strong reason to exist.
Aave is one of those protocols.
It is not the loudest name in the market, but it remains one of the most important lending platforms in crypto. Users deposit assets, borrow against collateral, manage liquidity, and access credit without relying on traditional banking rails.
That sounds simple, but this is one of the core ideas behind DeFi.
Capital should be programmable.
Liquidity should be available onchain.
Borrowing and lending should not be limited to closed financial systems.
This is where Aave continues to stand out.
When people talk about DeFi, they often focus only on yield. But Aave is bigger than that. It is infrastructure for onchain credit markets.
Stablecoin users can borrow. #ETH  holders can unlock liquidity without selling. Institutions can study how decentralized lending works at scale. Developers can build on top of existing money markets instead of starting from zero.
Aave also benefits from one of the strongest trends in crypto: the growth of stablecoins.
As more stablecoin liquidity moves onchain, lending markets become more important. People need places to deposit, borrow, hedge, rotate capital, and use liquidity efficiently. Aave sits directly inside that flow.
For AAVE, the token story is tied to the importance of the protocol itself.
The more DeFi matures, the more valuable serious lending infrastructure becomes. And Aave has already survived multiple market cycles, liquidity shocks, and periods when people claimed #defi  was dead.
That matters.
Because in crypto, survival is underrated.
Anyone can look strong during a bull market. The real test is staying relevant after the noise disappears.
Aave has done that.
Of course, AAVE is still a crypto asset. The price can be volatile, competition is real, and DeFi always carries smart contract and market risks.
But if the next stage of crypto is about useful financial infrastructure, then lending will remain one of the most important categories.
And Aave is still one of the strongest names in that category.
The market may rotate through new narratives every few weeks.
But DeFi needs credit markets.
Credit markets need liquidity.
And #AAVE  is still sitting at the center of that conversation.

Levels on a chart do, and right now the levels on ETH are the ones that demand a plan.

The 72-hour support on ETH is $1,728.95. That is roughly 23 dollars below the current print. Not a lot of room. The 72-hour resistance sits at $1,833.40, about 82 dollars overhead. So the trade range is compressed into a roughly 105-dollar window, and ETH is parked in the lower third of it. That positioning alone tells you where the immediate pressure sits: sellers have been leaning, and buyers have not yet reclaimed enough ground to shift momentum.

For BTC, the picture is steadier. Support at $61,306.84 is nearly $1,450 below the current price, offering a more comfortable cushion. Resistance at $64,700 sits just under $2,000 above. Bitcoin is midrange, which is textbook neutral. Neither bulls nor bears have an edge on the daily tape. That is not where you find urgency; it is where you wait.

ETH, though, is where the urgency lives.

Here is the risk framework a disciplined trader should be running right now. If ETH holds $1,728.95 on a retest, the floor remains intact and the range stays valid. That is the scenario where a defined-risk long near support makes structural sense, because your invalidation is the level itself. Lose it on a closing basis, and the thesis changes immediately. On the flip side, if ETH reclaims $1,833.40, the range resolves upward and the prior resistance becomes the new floor for continuation. That is the cleaner momentum trade, but it has not happened yet. Patience is the cheaper position.

When capital flows into ETH-adjacent infrastructure while ETH itself bleeds, it often signals that informed money is positioning ahead of a directional move. It does not guarantee the move is up. That said, risk management is not about predicting direction. It is about defining exposure before the move happens. Size any position so that a breach of $1,728.95 costs you an amount you are genuinely comfortable losing. If you cannot define that number before you enter, you are not trading; you are hoping.

The headlines around you are noise. StarkWare proposing changes to Bitcoin's supply schedule, EU regulatory votes, new payment licenses in Australia — none of this changes what the chart is telling you in the next 72 hours. Price is truth. Levels are the language.

Here is what the tape is telling futures traders at this exact moment: $BTC sits at $62,723.70 on Binance, down 0.69 percent over the last 24 hours, while $ETH prints $1,753.63, off 0.85 percent in the same window. But when you layer the derivatives picture on top, a more interesting story emerges, one about positioning, conviction, and the levels where the next real decision happens.

Start with the mechanism most traders overlook. Perpetual futures funding rates reflect which side of the market is paying to hold its position. When funding turns heavily positive, longs are paying shorts, which signals crowded bullish positioning and a market that is leveraged to the upside. When funding goes negative, the reverse is true. Right now both $BTC and $ETH are trading near flat after a slow grind lower, and the subtle read here is that the market is not aggressively positioned in either direction. That matters because low conviction in the derivatives market often precedes a directional move. The coiled spring analogy is tired, but it applies. Someone will be wrong soon.

The real numbers anchor the trade. For $BTC, the 72-hour support sits at $61,306.84, roughly 2.3 percent below the current print, and resistance caps the range at $64,700.00, about 3.1 percent above. That is a tight corridor. If $BTC holds above $61,306.84, the defense is intact and dip-buyers still control the lower boundary. If that level breaks on volume, the unwind accelerates because derivatives traders sitting on thin margins get liquidated in a cascade. On the flip side, a clean push through $64,700.00 flips the script entirely, signaling that spot demand is absorbing the leverage selling. Right now price is parked almost exactly in the middle of that range, which is exactly why derivatives positioning tells you more than spot alone.

$ETH paints a similar picture but with tighter compression. Current price $1,753.63 against a 72-hour support of $1,728.95 and resistance at $1,833.40. That is barely 1.4 percent of downside room to support and 4.5 percent to the top of the range. The asymmetry is noteworthy. If $ETH holds the $1,728.95 floor, the risk-reward skews favorably for a bounce toward resistance. If it loses that level, the path opens toward deeper unwinds, especially given $ETH open interest on perpetuals has been climbing even as price drifts. Open interest rising while price falls is the derivatives market's way of saying new shorts are entering, not just longs closing. That distinction is critical because new shorts create the fuel for a short squeeze if support holds.

What ties this together is how the broader market context shapes leverage behavior. For $ETH, the $1,728.95 support is the line where derivatives positioning either unwinds or squeezes. title: Binance Hiring General Manager to Drive West Africa Expansion
subTitle:
Binance Blends Growth Strategy With Regulatory Engagement
Binance is hiring a General Manager for West Africa as part of its Africa business development team. Announced on July 6 via the company's X account, the remote, full-time position is designed to support both business growth and regulatory engagement across the region.
The successful candidate will be responsible for developing a regional growth strategy that aligns with Binance's global objectives while adapting to local market conditions. Key responsibilities include identifying new business opportunities, leading market expansion initiatives, and overseeing cross-functional teams.
Regulatory collaboration is a major focus of the role. The General Manager will work closely with Binance's legal and compliance teams to coordinate documentation, manage approval processes, and maintain relationships with regulators across West Africa.
Binance Strengthens Its Presence Across West Africa
Binance has established a presence in several West African markets, including Ghana, Ivory Coast, Senegal, Togo, and Benin, although available services vary by country.
In many of these markets, users can purchase cryptocurrencies through localized payment methods such as mobile money. The exchange also supports peer-to-peer trading in regional currencies, including the West African CFA franc and the Ghanaian cedi.
Nigeria remains an exception after Binance suspended all services involving the Nigerian naira following increased regulatory scrutiny. Despite those restrictions, the company continues expanding its African footprint through local payment solutions, educational programs, community initiatives, and trading campaigns.
Leadership, Compliance, and Market Growth at the Core
Beyond business development, the new General Manager will serve as Binance's public representative across West Africa, managing relationships with government agencies, regulators, industry stakeholders, and local communities. The position also involves participating in policy discussions, engaging with key stakeholders, and representing the company at industry conferences and events.
Binance is seeking candidates with at least 10 years of senior management experience, preferably in business development or market expansion. The ideal applicant should have a strong understanding of regulatory frameworks, government relations, policymaking, and strategic growth initiatives.
The role also carries responsibility for profit and loss management, budgeting, performance oversight, and operational improvements. Binance has not disclosed the salary, reporting structure, preferred location within West Africa, or the expected hiring timeline.
